target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and safety.
objection: AI may offer some benefits, but it is not good for society overall because it harms people and businesses economically, erodes critical thinking, amplifies racism through biased outputs, and creates serious privacy risks that outweigh the benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is not good for society overall because of economic harm, critical-thinking erosion, racism, and privacy risks.
objection: Those harms do not justify rejecting AI outright, because they are implementation problems that can be reduced by responsible design and governance: AI can augment workers instead of replacing them, tutoring can be built to support reasoning, bias can be mitigated with audits and oversight, and privacy can be protected with data minimization and regulation.

target: AG1’s suggestion that responsible implementation can solve AI’s harms.
objection: The harms are structural and incentive-driven, not just technical bugs, so implementation fixes do not undercut the opposition: firms are rewarded for automation and cost-cutting, users will still outsource reasoning, fairness controls can fail as models and contexts change, and privacy protections are undermined by business models built on data collection.

target: AG2’s claim that structural incentives make AI harmful overall.
objection: That overgeneralizes from the current market to what society could choose, because policy and design controls can redirect incentives, require augmentation-first deployment, enforce learning workflows that preserve critical thinking, and add privacy-preserving technical safeguards.

target: AG1’s claim that governance and technical safeguards can make AI benefits outweigh harms.
objection: Safeguards are not reliable enough to prevent harm because AI systems are hard to audit, accountability is unclear when harm occurs, companies can deploy first and fix later, trust and information integrity erode through AI-generated content, and privacy leaks and inference risks remain even with mitigation.

target: AG2’s claim that safeguards cannot reliably solve AI’s risks.
objection: The fact that perfect guarantees are impossible does not mean AI should be rejected, because society already manages high-impact technologies with layered defenses and enforceable responsibility; transparency tools, targeted regulation, provenance mechanisms, and verification-focused design can make AI beneficial overall.

target: AG1’s claim that risk-tiering, provenance, and governance can control AI’s harms.
objection: AI risk is not static or fully measurable, and enforcement is structurally limited: model behavior changes with data and prompts, transparency artifacts often do not reveal real responsibility, watermarks and citations can be evaded or forged, and privacy mitigations do not eliminate memorization, leakage, or re-identification risk.

target: AG2’s claim that AI safeguards cannot reliably prevent harm.
objection: Society can use defense-in-depth: independent audits, regulator access, incident reporting, liability rules, continuous monitoring, rollback mechanisms, and verification tools can improve accountability and information integrity without rejecting AI outright.

target: AG1’s claim that audits, monitoring, and liability can keep AI beneficial.
objection: Even with strong governance, AI creates irreversible lock-in and dependency: schools, workplaces, and agencies will deskill users and concentrate power in a few firms faster than oversight can keep up, permanently weakening critical thinking, bargaining power, and democratic accountability.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably causes lock-in, deskilling, and power concentration.
objection: Those effects are not inevitable because phased rollout, human capability requirements, AI literacy, rollback triggers, interoperability standards, procurement rules, antitrust enforcement, and support for public-interest models can prevent or reduce dependency and concentration.

target: AG1’s claim that rollout policies and market rules can prevent lock-in and concentration.
objection: Those mitigations are unlikely to be implemented quickly enough and are easy to game: governance capacity lags behind adoption, students can fake comprehension, and interoperability or antitrust reforms move too slowly relative to how quickly AI becomes embedded in institutions.

target: AG2’s claim that real-world constraints make broad AI benefits irrelevant.
objection: The argument ignores distributional gains, because many of AI’s most valuable uses are direct, immediate benefits—especially accessibility tools for disabled people, communication and navigation help, and health-support tools—so the right response is targeted, opt-in, accessibility-first adoption rather than rejection.

target: AG1’s claim that accessibility-first, opt-in AI avoids the major harms.
objection: Accessibility use does not escape the structural problems: assistive tools still rely on sensitive data and monitoring, opt-in/opt-out becomes meaningless when AI becomes default infrastructure, and beneficial AI can still reproduce unequal treatment against racial minorities through biased outputs.

target: AG2’s claim that accessibility-first AI magnifies privacy and autonomy harms.
objection: Accessibility tools can be privacy-preserving with on-device processing, limited retention, and explicit user controls, and if AI-mediated services become effectively mandatory, rights-based policy can require real alternatives and a right to refuse AI without losing access.

target: AG1’s claim that assistive AI can be made privacy-preserving and choice-preserving.
objection: Those conditions are difficult to guarantee in practice because accessibility tools often become data pipelines under market pressure to collect more user data, privacy-preserving architecture does not stop upstream training and telemetry risks, and “rights to refuse” become nominal when AI is bundled into default services.

target: AG2’s claim that AI misuse risk makes AI net harmful overall.
objection: Misuse risk can be managed because AI’s harmful uses can also be countered by scaled detection, verification, and friction, while workplace safety can be protected by reducing automation bias and designing high-stakes workflows with human judgment.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits outweigh misuse and safety risks.
objection: Bias in AI decision-making can become self-reinforcing feedback loops in hiring, lending, policing, and school placement, where biased outputs shape future data and entrench algorithmic redlining while harmed people lack meaningful ways to contest decisions.

target: AG2’s claim that algorithmic redlining makes AI harmful overall.
objection: Biased feedback loops can themselves be detected and interrupted with continuous bias auditing, fairness-aware thresholds, retraining or rollback requirements, and meaningful human oversight plus appeal processes.

target: AG1’s claim that fairness auditing and appeal processes can break discriminatory feedback loops.
objection: In practice those mechanisms are too shallow, gameable, and under-enforced: fairness metrics can miss real harm, organizations can tune systems to pass tests without fixing injustice, and many affected people cannot realistically use appeal channels.

target: AG2’s claim that fairness governance is too weak to prevent discrimination.
objection: Governance can move beyond box-checking by using causal, outcome-based evaluation, continuous third-party oversight, mandatory disclosure, and built-in contestation and remedies, making bias harder to hide while preserving AI’s benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that stronger audits and contestation can solve fairness problems.
objection: Even perfect fairness/privacy governance for individual decisions does not address AI’s broader society-level harm: it lowers the cost of mass persuasion and manipulation by enabling tailored propaganda, while provenance labeling and platform rules cannot stop strategic misuse at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily enables unmanageable mass manipulation.
objection: The same technology can improve verification and add friction against misuse through deepfake detection, provenance signals, stronger labeling, audit logs, and platform accountability, so the proper conclusion is targeted anti-manipulation policy rather than rejecting AI overall.

target: AG1’s claim that verification and policy friction can control AI-driven manipulation.
objection: Verification cannot keep up with manipulation at scale because adversaries can iterate quickly, people still bear the cognitive burden of sorting truth from synthetic content, and platform incentives favor engagement over careful verification, creating a persistent trust-erosion externality.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms outweigh its benefits under realistic deployment.
objection: AI’s growing compute footprint is an additional externality: training and running large models consume significant energy and cooling resources, impose uneven environmental burdens on less powerful communities, and remain unsustainable even if safety safeguards improve.
